_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Mathematics unit lecture film, Lesson 2 Coins and Change. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson's own steps in order - Know your money, Count what is in the purse, Make this exact amount and The fewest pieces, Writing money, Which purse is worth more, How much more - and use the lesson's own worked examples: the 50, 20 and 5 purse counted to 75 sh, 35 sh built as 20, 10 and 5, 70 sh as a 50 and a 20 against seven 10s, 45 sh written three ways, the purse pair 20+20+5 against a single 50, and counting on from 35 sh to 50 sh in hops of 5 and 10. Money is written the way the lesson writes it, 45 sh, with KSh 45 named as the other way the shops write it.
title: Coins and Change
subtitle: Grade 2 Mathematics
objectives: Recognise value and money notation used in local currency.
Compare values of different combinations of coins or notes.
Recognise complements of 20 and complements of multiples of 10 (up to 100).

beats.say: This is money. The round ones are coins. The flat ones are notes.
Every piece has its own value. Count them all up, and you know what the purse is worth.
Our money is shillings. Every coin and note has its value printed on it.
These are the coins: one, five, ten, twenty and fifty shillings.

at.list: one, five, ten, twenty and fifty

beats.say: This flat one is a note. A note is worth more than most coins. This one is 100.

at.note: This flat one is a note

beats.say: A big coin is not always worth more. Read the number, not the size.

scenes.heading: Count what is in the purse

beats.say: Here is a purse with money in it. What is it all worth?
Always start with the biggest piece. Here the biggest is the 50.
Then count on. Fifty, and twenty more makes seventy.
Five more makes seventy-five. So the purse holds 75 sh.
Three pieces, and 75 shillings. Count the value, not the pieces.
Now you choose the money yourself. Make 35 sh exactly.
Take a 20, then a 10, then a 5. That is 35.
Say the total as you go: twenty, thirty, thirty-five.
Now make 70 sh, with as few pieces as you can.
A 50 fits, and leaves 20. A 20 finishes it, so two pieces.
Seven 10 shilling coins make 70 too, but that is seven pieces.
Money has its own way of being written down.
Forty-five shillings is written 45 sh, with the sh after it.
A shop may write KSh 45 instead, with the KSh in front.
Both mean the same money. Read the number first, then the letters.
Here are two purses. Which one is worth more?
Purse A holds a 20, a 20 and a 5. Add them up: 45 sh.
Purse B holds just one coin, a 50. That is 50 sh.
Purse B has fewer pieces and more money. More coins is not more money.
You have 35 sh, and the thing you want costs 50 sh.
Count on from what you have, up to the price.
Hop 5 to reach 40. Then hop 10 to reach 50.
The hops are 5 and 10. So you need 15 shillings more.
Count money biggest first, then count on from there.
One amount can be made in many ways. The fewest pieces uses the biggest coins.
45 sh and KSh 45 are two ways to write the same money.
Compare purses by value, and count on to find how much more.
